lead: An AC-AC converter turns one AC waveform into another: the same 50 Hz at a smaller RMS value, or a completely different frequency, with no DC link in between. After this unit you can work out the output voltage, current and power of a phase-controlled dimmer, an on-off heater controller, a PWM AC chopper, a cycloconverter and a matrix converter, and pick the right one for a given job.
about: This unit covers circuits that change an AC supply into another AC supply directly, without a DC link. Chapter 5.1 sets up the single-phase AC voltage controller and its two control laws, phase control and on-off control. Chapter 5.2 puts a TRIAC and a DIAC in that circuit and works through gate triggering in all four quadrants. Chapter 5.3 repeats the controller on three phases, where the phases interact because the neutral is gone. Chapter 5.4 replaces phase delay with high-frequency PWM, so the harmonics move up in frequency. Chapter 5.5 goes further and uses two phase-controlled groups to make a new output frequency, the cycloconverter. Chapter 5.6 closes with the matrix converter, nine switches that do the same job with no DC link at all.

chapters.idea: An AC voltage controller is a thyristor pair in series with the load; delaying the firing angle in each half cycle, or passing whole cycles and blocking whole cycles, sets the RMS voltage the load receives.
chapters.depth: The circuit: two SCRs back to back, or one TRIAC, in series with the load. Phase control: delay firing by the angle α in every half cycle, 0 ≤ α ≤ 180° for a resistive load, with V_rms = V_s√(1 − α/π + sin 2α/2π), where V_s is the supply RMS voltage and α is in radians. On-off (integral-cycle, burst) control: conduct for n whole cycles and block for m, duty D = n/(n+m), V_rms = V_s√D. Compare the two: phase control puts low-order current harmonics on the supply and gives a poor input power factor at large α; on-off control keeps the current sinusoidal but flickers at the burst rate. Cover R and RL loads and the conduction angle of an RL load. Applications: lamp dimming, heater and furnace control, fan regulators, induction motor soft starters. Some syllabi call this an AC voltage regulator.

figure.aria: A falling curve shows the RMS output ratio dropping from 1 at zero firing angle to 0 at 180 degrees, with a flat line at 0.707 crossing it exactly at 90 degrees.

chapters.example: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 20 Ω resistive load through a single-phase AC voltage controller. Find the RMS output voltage, the RMS current and the load power for (a) phase control at α = 90°, (b) on-off control with duty cycle D = 0.5. Answer: (a) V_rms = 230 × √(1 − 90/180 + sin 180°/(2π)) = 230 × √0.5 = 162.6 V; I = 162.6/20 = 8.13 A; P = 162.6²/20 = 1.32 kW. (b) V_rms = 230 × √0.5 = 162.6 V; I = 8.13 A; P = 1.32 kW. Same heating, very different harmonics.
chapters.trap: Putting the angle in degrees into a formula derived in radians. α = 90° must enter as π/2; the bracket then gives 0.5, so the ratio is 0.707, not 0.9.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the SCR and its natural commutation; Unit 2 for the meaning of firing angle in a controlled rectifier.
chapters.leave: Device physics, gate drive circuits and snubbers (Unit 1); rectifier load analysis and ripple calculations (Unit 2).

chapters.idea: A TRIAC conducts in both directions, so one three-terminal device plus one trigger network replaces the two-SCR pair, but the gate pulse polarity must suit the MT2 polarity.
chapters.depth: TRIAC structure as two SCRs in antiparallel sharing one gate referred to MT1; terminals MT1 and MT2. The four triggering quadrants are the four combinations of MT2 polarity and gate current polarity. Positive and negative gate pulse triggering, and why a short pulse is enough once the device latches and stays on until the current falls below the holding current. Gate sensitivity differs between quadrants: triggering is easiest when the gate current has the same polarity as MT2. Trigger circuits: RC phase-shift network with a DIAC (breaks over near 30 V and delivers a sharp pulse), UJT and PUT triggering, opto-isolated and zero-crossing drive. RC snubber across MT1-MT2, false triggering from dv/dt, latching and holding current. Worked dimmer for an incandescent lamp.

figure.title: TRIAC triggering quadrants
figure.aria: A four-row table lists the MT2 polarity, gate polarity and gate sensitivity for quadrants Q1 to Q4, with the two sensitive quadrants marked.

chapters.example: A 230 V, 50 Hz, 100 W incandescent lamp is dimmed by a TRIAC with a DIAC trigger network set to fire at α = 90°. Find the lamp resistance, the RMS voltage across it, the RMS current and the power delivered. Answer: R = V²/P = 230²/100 = 529 Ω; V_rms = 230 × 0.707 = 162.6 V; I = 162.6/529 = 0.307 A; P = 162.6²/529 = 50 W, half brightness at half power.
chapters.trap: Naming the quadrant from the gate polarity alone. A positive gate pulse with MT2 positive is quadrant 1, but the same positive pulse with MT2 negative is quadrant 4, the least sensitive one.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for TRIAC and DIAC structure and latching; Chapter 5.1 for the phase-control waveform and its RMS formula.
chapters.leave: SCR two-transistor model and commutation types (Unit 1); three-phase TRIAC circuits (Chapter 5.3).

chapters.idea: Three single-phase controllers on a three-phase supply interact through the load, because in a three-wire star or a delta there is no neutral to carry the zero-sequence current.
chapters.depth: Three configurations. First, three separate single-phase controllers in star with the neutral brought out: each phase is independent, 0 ≤ α ≤ 180°, and zero-sequence current returns in the neutral. Second, the usual three-phase three-wire star with six thyristors: for a resistive load the output is the full supply for α ≤ 60°, conduction becomes discontinuous above 60°, and the output falls to zero at α = 150°. Third, the delta connection with six thyristors, used for high-current loads. Symmetrical and asymmetrical firing, line and phase quantities, input current harmonics, and why triplen harmonics do not appear in the line currents of a three-wire load. Applications: three-phase heaters, motor soft starters, static switches for capacitor banks. Some syllabi call this a three-phase AC voltage regulator.

figure.title: Three-phase controller, star load
figure.aria: A three-phase supply feeds one controlled thyristor pair per phase, the three pairs join at a star load, and a dashed link shows a neutral that exists only in the four-wire circuit.

chapters.example: A 415 V, 50 Hz, three-phase supply feeds a star-connected resistive load of 10 Ω per phase through a three-phase AC voltage controller. (a) For α = 60°, find the RMS phase voltage, the line current and the total power. (b) At what firing angle does the output fall to zero? Answer: (a) at α = 60° conduction is just continuous, so the phase voltage is the full supply value V_ph = 415/√3 = 239.6 V; I = 239.6/10 = 23.96 A; P = 3 × 239.6²/10 = 17.2 kW. (b) Zero output at α = 150°.
chapters.trap: Using the single-phase formula on each phase of a three-wire star load. With no neutral the three phase currents must sum to zero, so changing one firing angle changes the voltage on the other two phases.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1 for the single-phase controller, Unit 1 for SCR pairs, Unit 2 for three-phase source quantities.
chapters.leave: Three-phase rectifier analysis (Unit 2); three-phase inverter conduction modes (Unit 4).

chapters.idea: A PWM AC chopper switches the load between the supply and a short at a frequency far above 50 Hz, so the duty ratio sets the RMS voltage and the unwanted frequencies sit high, where a small filter removes them.
chapters.depth: The single-phase PWM AC chopper: two bidirectional switches, one in series with the load and one freewheeling across the load, driven complementarily with a dead time so the supply is never shorted. Duty ratio D = t_on/T; RMS output V_s√D; fundamental D·V_s; harmonics clustered around the switching frequency and its multiples. Why the input current stays close to sinusoidal and the input power factor stays high, unlike phase control. Choosing the switching frequency against device losses, and the small input filter that follows. Three-phase versions in brief. Applications: AC voltage stabilisers and dynamic voltage restorers, solid-state tap changers, fast lamp dimming, motor soft starting. Some syllabi call this an AC chopper or a switched-mode AC controller.

figure.aria: Two switching periods of 100 microseconds show the series switch on for the first 50 microseconds and the freewheel switch on for the next 50, with the load voltage alternating between supply voltage and zero.

chapters.example: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 50 Ω resistive load through a PWM AC chopper with a freewheeling switch. The switching frequency is 10 kHz and the duty ratio is D = 0.6. Find the RMS output voltage, the output power and where the lowest output harmonics lie. Answer: V_rms = V_s√D = 230 × √0.6 = 178.2 V; P = 178.2²/50 = 635 W; the lowest harmonics sit near the 10 kHz switching frequency, about 200 times the supply frequency.
chapters.trap: Writing V_o = D·V_s and calling it RMS. D·V_s is the fundamental component; the RMS value of the chopped waveform is V_s√D, which is always larger.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1 for the phase-control baseline, Unit 1 for IGBT and MOSFET switches, Unit 4 for PWM ideas.
chapters.leave: Inverter PWM and harmonic elimination (Unit 4); switching loss and heat sink design (Unit 1).

chapters.idea: A cycloconverter connects the load to the supply through two phase-controlled converter groups, one for each output half cycle, and slowly modulates their firing angles so the average output follows a sine of a different frequency.
chapters.depth: Single-phase to single-phase cycloconverter: two phase-controlled bridges in antiparallel, the positive group conducting for the positive half of the output and the negative group for the negative half. The firing angle of the conducting group is modulated slowly so the average output follows a sine of the wanted frequency. Circulating-current mode with an intergroup reactor against non-circulating mode where only one group conducts and the other is held blocked. Cosine-wave crossing control for the firing angle. Step-down operation with f_o < f_s and a practical quality limit of about f_o ≤ f_s/3. Step-up operation with f_o > f_s, which needs forced commutation and gives a poor waveform with subharmonics. RL load behaviour, discontinuous current and the input displacement factor. Applications: low-speed high-torque drives such as cement kilns, rolling mills and ship propulsion.

figure.aria: A timeline shows the positive converter group conducting for 20 milliseconds and then the negative group for the next 20, giving one 40 millisecond output cycle at 25 hertz from a 50 hertz supply.

chapters.example: A single-phase step-down cycloconverter feeds an R = 10 Ω, L = 20 mH load from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. The fundamental output voltage is 200 V RMS at 12.5 Hz. Find the frequency ratio, the output period, the load current and the power. Answer: f_o/f_s = 12.5/50 = 0.25, inside the 1/3 limit; output period = 1/12.5 = 80 ms; X_L = 2π × 12.5 × 0.02 = 1.571 Ω; Z = √(10² + 1.571²) = 10.12 Ω; I = 200/10.12 = 19.8 A; P = I²R = 19.8² × 10 = 3.9 kW.
chapters.trap: Drawing a DC link or a smoothing capacitor in the middle of a cycloconverter, or claiming any output frequency is possible. There is no DC link, and good step-down quality needs f_o at most about f_s/3.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for phase-controlled converters and their average output voltage; Chapter 5.1 for firing-angle control.
chapters.leave: Rectifier average-voltage derivations (Unit 2); dual-converter circulating current theory (Unit 2).

chapters.idea: Nine bidirectional switches connect any input phase to any output phase, so one array sets both the amplitude and the frequency of the output with no DC link and no stored energy.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it to an introduction plus the worked R-load design. The 3×3 array of nine bidirectional switches, every input phase connectable to every output phase. Two hard rules: never close two switches in the same column, which shorts two supply phases, and never leave an output leg open. Modulation by duty cycles computed from the input voltages (scalar or Venturini method) or by space vectors. Maximum voltage transfer ratio 0.866 in the linear range. Input filter for the chopped currents, four-step current-direction commutation, natural regeneration, and the absence of a DC-link capacitor as the main commercial advantage. Comparison with a back-to-back inverter. Applications: compact motor drives, wind power and aerospace supplies.

figure.title: 3×3 switch matrix
figure.aria: A three-by-three table of switches S1 to S9, one row per output phase and one column per input phase, with one closed switch marked in each output row and no two in the same column.

chapters.example: A 415 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a star-connected R = 20 Ω per phase load through a three-phase matrix converter with voltage transfer ratio q = 0.5 and output frequency 30 Hz. Find the output phase voltage, the output current and the power, and check the design. Answer: V_ph,in = 415/√3 = 239.6 V; V_o = q × 239.6 = 119.8 V; I = 119.8/20 = 5.99 A; P = 3 × 119.8²/20 = 2.15 kW; q = 0.5 is below the 0.866 limit, so the design is valid.
chapters.trap: Asking for q = 1 and expecting a sine output. The linear limit is 0.866, and a duty cycle that closes two switches in one column short-circuits the supply.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for bidirectional switches; Chapter 5.4 for PWM chopping and Chapter 5.5 for the idea of building a new frequency by switching.
chapters.leave: Space vector modulation for inverters (Unit 4); device protection and thermal design (Unit 1).
